summary.text: For an arbitrary bound \(N\), take \(M=\max(3,N+2)\) and \(n=(M+1)!/6\); positivity supplies \(n=x+y\) with \(p=6x-1\) Sophie Germain and \(q=6y-1,q+2\) twin primes. If \(p\le N\), then \(p\mid 6n\) and hence \(p\mid q+2=6n-p\), forcing \(p=q+2\), while if \(q\le N\), then \(q+2\mid 6n\) and hence \(q+2\mid p=6n-(q+2)\), forcing \(q+2=p\); both equalities are impossible modulo \(6\), so each family contains primes above every bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
T=\{q\in\mathbb N:q\text{ is prime and }q+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)=A227923(n)\) is the sum, over integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), of an indicator which is \(1\) precisely when, on putting \(y=n-x\), all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime. Thus, if \(a(n)>0\), at least one summand is nonzero. Consequently there are positive integers \(x,y\) with \(x+y=n\) such that
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\tag{1}
\]
are all prime. Indeed, \(1\le x<n\) implies \(y=n-x\ge1\). Notice also that if
\[
P=6x-1,
\]
then
\[
2P+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1,
\]
so the first two primality conditions in (1) say exactly that \(P\) is a Sophie Germain prime. Similarly, if
\[
Q=6y-1,
\]
then \(Q+2=6y+1\), so the last two conditions say that \(Q\) is the lower member of a twin-prime pair.

Assume now the hypothesis
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\tag{2}
\]
We shall prove that both \(S\) and \(T\) are unbounded. Since every finite set of natural numbers is bounded, this will prove that both sets are infinite.

Fix an arbitrary natural number \(N\). Set
\[
M=\max\{3,N+2\},\qquad F=(M+1)!,\qquad n=\frac{F}{6}.
\]
This quotient is an integer. Indeed, \(M\ge3\), so \(M+1\ge4\); hence \(4!=24\) divides \((M+1)!\), and in particular \(6\mid F\). We therefore have the exact identity
\[
6n=F.
\tag{3}
\]
Moreover, \(F\ge4!=24\), so \(n=F/6\ge4\), and in particular \(n>1\).

By (2), \(a(n)>0\). By the meaning of \(a(n)\) explained above, there are integers \(x,y\ge1\) such that
\[
x+y=n
\tag{4}
\]
and all four numbers in (1) are prime. For this decomposition define
\[
P=6x-1,
\qquad Q=6y-1,
\qquad R=6y+1=Q+2.
\tag{5}
\]
Then \(P\) and \(2P+1=12x-1\) are prime, so \(P\in S\). Also \(Q\) and \(Q+2=R\) are prime, so \(Q\in T\). We prove separately that \(P>N\) and \(Q>N\).

First suppose, for a contradiction, that
\[
P\le N.
\tag{6}
\]
Since \(N+2\le M\), this implies in particular that \(P\le M+1\). The positive integer \(P\) therefore occurs among the factors of \((M+1)!\), and hence
\[
P\mid F.
\tag{7}
\]
Using (3), (4), and (5), we compute
\[
F-P
 =6n-(6x-1)
 =6(x+y)-6x+1
 =6y+1
 =R.
\tag{8}
\]
Because \(P\mid F\) and, trivially, \(P\mid P\), equation (8) gives
\[
P\mid R.
\tag{9}
\]
But \(R\) is prime. Every positive divisor of a prime is either \(1\) or the prime itself, so (9) implies
\[
P=1\quad\text{or}\quad P=R.
\tag{10}
\]
The first possibility is impossible because \(P\) is prime, and hence \(P>1\). The second is also impossible: by (5),
\[
P=6x-1\equiv -1\equiv5\pmod 6,
\qquad
R=6y+1\equiv1\pmod 6.
\]
Thus \(P\ne R\). Both alternatives in (10) are impossible, contradicting (6). Therefore
\[
P>N.
\tag{11}
\]
Since \(P\in S\), we have found a Sophie Germain prime larger than the arbitrary bound \(N\).

We next prove that the lower twin prime \(Q\) also exceeds \(N\). Suppose instead that
\[
Q\le N.
\tag{12}
\]
Its twin partner is \(R=Q+2\), so
\[
R\le N+2\le M\le M+1.
\tag{13}
\]
The number \(R\) is positive and at most \(M+1\), and hence it divides the factorial:
\[
R\mid F.
\tag{14}
\]
Again using (3), (4), and (5), this time subtracting \(R\), we obtain
\[
F-R
 =6n-(6y+1)
 =6(x+y)-6y-1
 =6x-1
 =P.
\tag{15}
\]
Since \(R\mid F\) and \(R\mid R\), equation (15) yields
\[
R\mid P.
\tag{16}
\]
The number \(P\) is prime, so a positive divisor of \(P\) must be \(1\) or \(P\). Therefore
\[
R=1\quad\text{or}\quad R=P.
\tag{17}
\]
The first alternative is impossible because \(R\) is prime and therefore greater than \(1\). The second alternative is impossible for the same congruence reason as before:
\[
R=6y+1\equiv1\pmod6,
\qquad
P=6x-1\equiv5\pmod6.
\]
Thus (17) is impossible, contradicting (12). It follows that
\[
Q>N.
\tag{18}
\]
As \(Q\in T\), this gives a lower member of a twin-prime pair larger than \(N\).

We have shown that for every natural number \(N\), there exists a Sophie Germain prime \(P>N\), and there exists a lower twin prime \(Q>N\). Hence both \(S\) and \(T\) are unbounded subsets of the natural numbers. A finite subset of \(\mathbb N\) has a largest element and is therefore bounded, so neither \(S\) nor \(T\) can be finite. Consequently there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
